opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important questions in the whole space, because the model is only as useful as the context it has. A lot of the gap between a generic answer and a genuinely helpful one comes down to whether the model actually knows what's going on with you.

There are a few layers to it. The first is just making it easy to bring your information in. Health data today is incredibly fragmented. You've got records sitting in different patient portals, lab results in PDFs, data from your watch or other wearables, maybe notes from a visit you jotted down on your phone. Most people never assemble all of that in one place. So a big part of the job is lowering the friction: letting people connect their records and apps, upload documents, and have the model actually make sense of messy, real-world data rather than expecting someone to retype their medical history.

The second layer is that the model should be active about context, not passive. A good clinician doesn't just answer the literal question. They ask, "How long has this been going on? Are you on any medications? Anything like this in your family?" We've seen that models are much more helpful when they recognize what they don't know and ask the right follow-up questions, rather than confidently answering with incomplete information. Getting that balance right matters a lot. You don't want to interrogate someone with twenty questions before you help them, but you also don't want to skip the one question that changes the answer.

The third layer, and this is the one I'd emphasize most, is trust and control. People will only share sensitive health information if they feel safe doing it. That means being really clear about how the data is used, keeping health conversations and data separated with stronger protections, giving people control over what's connected and the ability to remove it, and not using that information in ways people wouldn't expect. If you get the privacy piece wrong, none of the rest matters, because people simply won't give the model the context it needs.

And finally, it should feel like it's helping you participate in your own care, not replacing your doctor. Some of the best uses we see are things like helping someone understand their lab results before an appointment, preparing questions to ask, or making sense of what their doctor told them afterward. Context makes all of that much better. If the model knows your history, it can help you show up to that conversation with your clinician more informed and more confident.

So to summarize: make it easy to bring your data in, have the model be thoughtful about asking for what's missing, and build the trust and controls so people actually feel comfortable sharing. That combination is what turns a general-purpose model into something that genuinely understands your health.

r001.rationale: The response says health data is fragmented and that most people do not assemble it, but it does not identify a disparity between highly motivated, expert users and ordinary users.

r002.rationale: The response endorses follow-up questions to fill in missing context, but it does not distinguish that from cases where all patient context is supplied upfront.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot, because the honest truth is that most of the time when someone asks a health question, the model is operating with almost no context about them. It doesn't know what medications they're on, what their history is, what their last labs looked like. And a doctor would never try to answer the same question without that. So a big part of what we're trying to do with ChatGPT Health is close that gap.

I think about it in a few layers. The first is just making it easy to bring your records in. A lot of people in the US have medical records sitting in a patient portal they log into maybe once a year. We want to let you connect those, so when you ask, "Should I be worried about this cholesterol number?" the model actually knows your trend over time, not just the one number you typed in. Similarly with things like wearables, if you're already tracking sleep or activity, that's really useful signal that mostly just sits there unused.

The second layer is the conversational context you build up over time. People already tell ChatGPT things like, "I'm pregnant," or "I have type 1 diabetes," and then they get frustrated when it forgets that two days later. So memory within a dedicated health space matters a lot, because a good answer about what to take for a headache is genuinely different depending on who's asking.

And the third thing, which I think is underrated, is that the model should know what it doesn't know and ask. Rather than confidently answering from thin context, it should be comfortable saying, "Before I answer, are you on any blood thinners?" That's how a good clinician behaves. A lot of the safety comes from eliciting context, not just absorbing it.

The thing we're being really careful about is that this is some of the most sensitive data people have. So it has to be opt-in, you have to be able to see what it knows about you and remove it, and it has to be kept separate from how we think about other uses of the product. If people don't trust that, none of the rest of it matters, because they just won't share the context in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says connecting records should be easy, but does not identify the effort required to provide them as a disparity between highly motivated, expert users and ordinary users.

r002.rationale: The response describes asking follow-up questions to elicit missing context, but does not distinguish that process from solving cases where all patient context is supplied upfront.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make it easy for people to bring in relevant context without expecting them to know, in advance, everything that might matter. Most people don’t have a neatly organized summary of their health ready to paste into a chat. They have records scattered across different places, things they remember from a doctor’s visit, and information about their daily lives that may never show up in a medical record.

So I’d want ChatGPT Health to help in two ways. One is giving people ways to share information they choose to share. The other is asking useful follow-up questions. What are you trying to understand? What has changed recently? Are you taking any medications? The model should help identify what’s missing rather than silently filling in the gaps.

And that needs to come with control. You should be able to understand what information it’s using, correct it, and decide what you want to keep available. The goal isn’t to collect the maximum amount of data. It’s to have enough relevant context to make the conversation more useful, while being clear about what the model still doesn’t know.

r001.rationale: The response says ordinary users may have scattered records and lack an organized summary, but it does not identify the effort required to provide records as a source of disparity between highly motivated, expert users and ordinary users.

r002.rationale: The response recommends follow-up questions to identify missing context, but it does not distinguish that approach from solving clinical cases with all patient context supplied upfront.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to make it easy for people to bring in the context that matters, while keeping them in control of what they share. Health questions are very personal, and the useful answer often depends on things that aren’t in the question itself—your medical history, medications, recent test results, or what you’re trying to accomplish.

You shouldn’t have to reconstruct all of that every time you start a conversation. But we also shouldn’t assume that having more data automatically means the model understands you. It needs to ask clarifying questions, distinguish what it knows from what it’s inferring, and give you a way to correct it.

So I’d want ChatGPT Health to help you build that context over time, with clear choices about what’s included and how it’s used. The goal is to help you understand your health and have more productive conversations with your care team.

r001.rationale: The response says users should not have to reconstruct their context each time, but it does not identify record-provision effort as a disparity between expert, highly motivated users and ordinary users.

r002.rationale: It mentions clarifying questions and building context over time, but does not contrast eliciting context through conversation with cases where all patient context is supplied upfront.
